Text of Proposed Laws | 135
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 40 CONTINUED
reverberates: clinics close, families lose doctors, and
patients suffer needlessly from conditions that could
have been prevented or managed.
(h) Access to affordable, high-quality care saves lives,
shields families from crushing medical debt, and
strengthens communities. When coverage is lost or
diluted, hospitals and clinics are forced to make
impossible choices—cutting back on staff, restricting
services, or closing entire units—leaving whole
populations without a safety net and undermining the
health of all Californians.
(i) As Medi-Cal funding is threatened by reduced
federal funding and state appropriations, Californians
also face soaring private health insurance premiums.
These twin pressures only increase the number of
uninsured and underinsured, as employers scale back
benefits and disrupt dependent coverage, and as
individuals drop unaffordable health coverage.
(j) Every child in California deserves access to high
quality education. Today California public schools face
unprecedented uncertainty caused in part by cuts to
Medi-Cal and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance
Program (SNAP).
(k) In addition, current federal budget proposals for
2026 would impose deep cuts on overall funding to
public schools, particularly for high-need students,
rural schools, and disadvantaged communities.
(l) These federal disruptions arrive as California’s
schools are still reeling from recent state budget
shortfalls and looming payment deferrals. On top of
this, declining enrollment and enrollment-related
funding, rising costs, and increasing student needs are
putting school districts under mounting budgetary
pressure.
(m) More than 5 million Californians—among them,
children, families, seniors, and people with
disabilities—depend on the lifeline of CalFresh,
California’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance
Program (SNAP), to put food on the table in a state
where one in five experience hunger due to food
insecurity.
(n) The historic federal cuts to SNAP in recent federal
budget legislation will strip away billions of dollars in
vital food assistance from our most vulnerable
neighbors, translating into the loss of millions of meals
and deepening hunger across communities already
struggling to make ends meet.
(o) Robust evidence shows that SNAP and CalFresh
not only alleviate hunger, but also dramatically improve
health and educational outcomes for California’s
children, break cycles of poverty, and build stronger
futures for entire families.
(p) These cuts will further pressure already strained
state efforts and the limited resources of food banks
and local agencies such as CalFood and the California
Food Assistance Program.
(q) Collectively, these reductions in federal funding
and state appropriations impose compounding risks for
low- and moderate-income Californians seeking access
to essential health care, education and nutrition. They
also threaten California’s ability to plan for its future,
which requires continued investments in its critical
state programs.
(r) California has around 200 billionaires who
collectively possess an astonishing $2 trillion in wealth.
These billionaires pay less than 1.5% of their total
wealth in annual taxes, including federal, state, and
local taxes, according to leading economic
estimates—a small fraction of what ordinary
Californians pay.
(s) There are more than 19 million taxpayers in
California who are not billionaires. They include
working-class individuals such as nurses, teachers and
firefighters, as well as wealthier taxpayers like highly
compensated professionals, entrepreneurs, and tech
industry workers. All of these Californians pay tax on a
much larger portion of their true economic income than
the state’s billionaires do. According to economic
analysis and including all taxes at all levels of
government, billionaires pay 24% of their income in
taxes while the average taxpayer pays 30%. This means
that the average taxpayer pays a 25% larger share of
their economic income, taking into account all state
and federal taxes, than the average billionaire. See
Akcan Balkir, Emmanuel Saez, Danny Yagan, and
Gabriel Zucman, How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay?
Evidence from Administrative Data, National Bureau of
Economic Research Working Paper No. 34170 (2025).
(t) A wealth tax is not a new concept under California
law; narrower and less progressive wealth taxes are
already paid by wealthy and low-income Californians
alike. These taxes include the annual Vehicle License
Fee, a tax based on 0.65% of the value of a vehicle, and
the annual property tax on housing of about 1% on the
assessed value of a house.
(u) The immense and growing fortunes of billionaires
bring privileges inaccessible to most. Whereas nurses,
teachers, firefighters, and tech workers alike pay taxes
on nearly all of their earned income, billionaires can
shield enormous sums from taxation. Their primary
assets—stocks, businesses, real estate—grow in value
year after year, but because this growth is taxed only at
sale and billionaires often need not sell, they pay no tax
on their rising fortunes. Moreover, when these types of
assets are passed to heirs, current laws enable billions
of dollars in untaxed wealth to be inherited without ever
triggering an income tax bill. Many also employ
complex financial strategies to relocate wealth “on
paper” while, in reality, continuing to benefit from
California’s economy and infrastructure.
(v) Scholars have shown that closing these billionaire
loopholes is possible, practical and fair. They
demonstrate that carefully crafted policy can preserve
entrepreneurial success while safeguarding the state
economy and avoiding undue burden on administrators
or the broader taxpayer base. See Brian Galle, David
Gamage, and Darien Shanske, Money Moves: Taxing
the Wealthy at the State Level, 113 California Law
Review 635 (2025).

TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 40 CONTINUED
40
(w) Since the 1980s, the wealth of billionaires has
grown by an average 7% each year, vastly outpacing
the growth in wages and savings for ordinary
Californians. The collective wealth of California
billionaires has surged from $300 billion in 2011 to
$700 billion in 2019 to over $2 trillion in 2025. The
wealth tax imposed by this act would only modestly
slow this explosive growth, collecting less than the
billionaires typically gain in just a single year. California
billionaires, even after paying the tax, will continue to
amass ever-rising fortunes.
(x) According to leading economists, billionaire wealth
is more concentrated in California than in the United
States overall. As a result, the state is uniquely
positioned to address both the well-documented crisis
of wealth inequality in the United States and the
emerging and interrelated crises the state faces with
respect to health care, education and hunger-relief
programs.
(y) Billionaires have built their extraordinary fortunes
with the help of California resources and were the
largest beneficiaries of the federal legislation that
contributed to the current state budget crisis. It
therefore is both necessary and equitable to ask those
who have benefitted most from California’s resources
to contribute proportionately to support health care,
education, and nutrition in California through a one-
time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.
(z) In light of the emergency funding situation, to
ensure that revenues collected can be spent without
unnecessary delay, and to remove uncertainty created
from any legal challenges, the people have provided for
expedited judicial review of this act.
SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
(a) The purpose of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act,
referred to herein as the “act,” is to protect access to
high quality, equitable health care, and to support
funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public
education and food assistance programs, by raising
revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.
(b) Revenues from the act are intended to respond to
urgent, existing health care, education, and nutrition
needs that are being worsened by reductions in federal
and state funding and by broader fiscal uncertainty
facing the state.
(c) By designating billionaire wealth the source of this
critical revenue, the act confronts the fundamental
unfairness that arises because a large percentage of
billionaire wealth is never taxed by the state due to
billionaires’ unique ability to control the timing,
location, and amount of income tax that they pay.
(d) The act raises funding for health care, education,
and food assistance by imposing a narrowly applicable,
one-time tax that is administratively feasible and
efficient to enforce against all billionaires in the state.
(e) The act is intended to treat similarly situated
taxpayers and assets similarly, except to the extent that
sound tax policy requires otherwise.
136 | Text of Proposed Laws
SEC. 4. Section 37 is added to Article XIII of the
California Constitution, to read:
SEC. 37. (a) This section authorizes and enables a
one-time tax on the accumulated wealth of California
billionaires, imposed on those individuals who are
California residents within the meaning of Sections
17014 and 17015.5 of the Revenue and Taxation Code
as of the tax obligation date as defined in the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
(b) The following definitions apply to this section:
(1) “Act” refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
(2) “Reserve Fund” refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax
Reserve Fund, created by this act.
(c) Notwithstanding any other provision of the
Constitution, the act provides for taxation on all forms
of personal property and wealth, whether tangible or
intangible, and allows for the classification of personal
property and wealth for differential taxation or for
exemption, for the purpose of imposing the one-time
tax on the wealth of California billionaires. Personal
property and wealth that is so taxed includes, but is not
limited to, shares of capital stock, bonds or other
evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable
interest therein.
(d) The 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund is hereby
created in the State Treasury. All revenues from the act,
including taxes, interest, and penalties, and less
refunds, shall be deposited in the State Treasury by the
Controller to the credit of the Reserve Fund. After
accounting for administrative expenses as provided by
law, the Controller shall allocate and transfer the
remaining moneys in the Reserve Fund to the following
subaccounts, which are hereby created: 90% to the
Billionaire Tax Health Account and 10% to the Billionaire
Tax Education and Food Assistance Account. The
moneys in the Billionaire Tax Health Account and the
Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account
shall be allocated as provided by law.
(e) Notwithstanding any other law, the Reserve Fund is
a special fund, permanently separate and apart from
the General Fund or any other state fund or account.
The taxes and the moneys resulting from the act shall
not be considered to be part of the General Fund, as
that term is used in Chapter 1 (commencing with
Section 16300) of Part 2 of Division 4 of Title 2 of the
Government Code; and shall not be considered “General
Fund revenues,” “state revenues,” “moneys,” or
“proceeds of taxes” under Section 8 of Article XIII B for
the purposes of any section of Article XIII B, or Section 8
or 8.5 of Article XVI. Any revenue raised through the act
shall also not be considered “personal income taxes
paid on net capital gains” for purposes of Section 20 of
Article XVI. The taxes levied by this act are not “ad
valorem taxes on real property” for purposes of
Section 1 of Article XIII A. To the extent any provision of
Article XIII A would otherwise be construed to limit,
restrict, or apply to the rate, base, valuation, or
imposition of the tax authorized by this section, that
provision shall not apply to, and is superseded by, this
section. Notwithstanding Section 16305.7 of the
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 40 CONTINUED
Government Code, any interest or dividends earned on
moneys in the Reserve Fund shall be retained in the

1
PROPOSITION 40
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
Section-by-Section Summary
Introduction to this summary. This document has been prepared by the drafters of
Proposition 40, the California Billionaire Tax Act (“Prop 40”), to explain its details in
plain English to voters and other interested parties, such as legislators, regulators and
taxpayers. It is being submitted as public testimony and posted publicly.
This summary describes the ordinary meaning of Prop 40. California courts will use
ordinary principles of constitutional and statutory interpretation, including construing the
“plain and ordinary meaning,” to resolve any disputes about what Prop 40 does. Critics of
Prop 40 have posted claims about the measure that differ at points with this summary. In
our view these claims rest on implausible and often unreasonable efforts to twist the plain
language and intent of Prop 40. California courts have rejected the use of strained,
unreasonable arguments to conjure up ambiguity and thus these contrary accounts should
be rejected. In the event that courts do find some Prop 40 language ambiguous, we expect
they will rely in part on this summary and other interpretations offered by the drafters.
California courts attempt to honor voters’ intentions, and so have generally held drafters
to the claims about an initiative that they have made publicly to voters.1 In addition, a
ballot initiative that can be read and readily understood by voters cannot address every
conceivable complex legal question that might arise, and so the drafters expect that some
highly technical issues, such as the treatment of property held through single-member
LLCs, may be resolved through further guidance from California tax regulators.
Prop 40 Overview.2 The Act is a one-time wealth tax initiative for tax year 2026.
Revenues from the one-time tax are committed to address an urgent and pressing fiscal
emergency caused by the expected imminent loss of about $100 billion in federal funding
for health care, education, and nutrition programs. The tax portion of the Act (i) imposes
a 5% excise tax on California-resident billionaires on their worldwide net worth of as of
December 31, 2026, payable at once, or over 5 years with a deferral charge; (ii) defines a
California-resident billionaire as a billionaire who resided in California as of January 1,
2026; (iii) allows taxpayers who do not have cash available to pay the tax to defer
payment until later, with an interest charge; and (iv) further offers optional deferral
accounts for qualifying taxpayers.
Structure. The measure is implemented through (A) a constitutional amendment (new
Article XIII, Section 37) authorizing the tax and creating a dedicated Reserve Fund; (B) a
1 See, for example, Rossi v. Brown, 9 Cal.4th 688, 700 n. 7 (1995).
2 The drafters discuss the policy background for the Act and other issues here:
https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5996554.
2
Government Code article establishing Reserve Fund subaccounts and
appropriation/reporting rules for that fund that will be primarily dedicated to health care,
education, and nutrition programs; and (C) a new Part 27 of the Revenue and Taxation
Code providing the key tax rules.
Sec. 1. Title
Provides that Prop 40 may be cited as the “2026 Billionaire Tax Act.”
Sec. 2. Findings
The findings describe urgent and pressing (and in that sense, one-time) threats to
California’s health care, education, and nutrition assistance systems arising from an
expected $100 billion in federal funding cuts affecting Medi-Cal, California public
schools, and CalFresh/SNAP.
Sec. 3. Purpose and Intent
The purpose of Prop 40 is to raise revenue to fund health care, K-14 education, and food
assistance through levying a one-time, administrable, and fair tax on California
billionaires. The billionaire taxpayers are most able to pay the tax, and also generally pay
much less in taxes relative to their ability to pay compared to many other Californians.
Because there are urgent and pressing threats to California’s health care, education, and
nutrition assistance systems arising from an expected $100 billion in federal funding cuts,
and because a one-time tax can be set up and administered much more quickly to begin
raising revenues sooner, the one-time structure of the tax is best suited to the imminent
fiscal emergency.
Sec. 4. Constitutional Authorization and Dedicated Reserve Fund.
Section 4 adds Section 37 to the California Constitution, which grants constitutional
authorization for the wealth tax. As described in greater detail below, it also provides for
the creation of a Reserve Fund and permits facial challenges to the law to be adjudicated
through a validation action proceeding.
• Use of funds. California’s constitution contains numerous complicated fiscal
rules, including caps on state expenditures. Such rules and limits were not
designed to account for emergencies of the type created by recent massive federal
funding cuts. As a result of these cuts, California needs to significantly increase
its expenditures to maintain the same baseline of services. Accordingly, this
section assures that proceeds from Prop 40 will be expended to mitigate the
impact of the federal cuts. Proceeds from the tax are placed in a new Reserve
Fund that is permanently separate from the General Fund, with 90% committed to
health care; and 10% to K-14 education and food assistance, all for the benefit of
low and moderate-income families and individuals.
3
• Legal challenges. Generally, as a matter of California constitutional law,
challenges to taxation can only be made after a tax is paid. In order to provide for
more fiscal certainty for the Legislature, this section amends those rules to permit
certain legal challenges to be brought immediately and to have a speedier
resolution, through the California courts. The provision is based on validation
actions, described more in the discussion of Operative Tax Provisions at Section
50314.
Sec. 5. Reserve Fund Implementation in the Government Code.
Section 16355
Creates the operational rules for the Reserve Fund and its two subaccounts, the Health
Account and the Education and Food Assistance Account. The permitted uses of the tax
revenue in the subaccounts are defined broadly.
For the Health Account, which shall receive 90% of the tax revenue, permitted uses
include restoring or addressing reductions in federal funding or state appropriations;
protecting and enhancing Medi-Cal and other coverage programs; supporting safety net
providers; preventing or mitigating facility closures or service reductions; and other
investments supporting health care access, coverage, benefits, funding, services, and
provider payments.
As for the Education and Food Assistance Account, which shall receive 10% of the tax
revenue, permitted uses include education spending to restore or address reductions in
federal or state funding or to protect/enhance the K–14 public education system; and food
assistance spending to restore or address reductions in federal or state funding or to invest
in programs like CalFresh, and California’s Universal Meals Program.
This section also limits how much anticipated revenue the Legislature can spend in one
year (up to $25 billion/year) to provide for spending over a five-year period. It also
forbids the Legislature from using this new revenue to replace existing state funds.
At subdivision (e), the section provides funds for tax administration. The Franchise Tax
Board (“Board”) is charged with administering the tax. This section provides the Board
with a start-up loan of up to $50 million to implement Prop 40, as well as an ongoing
annual reimbursement from the Reserve Fund for actual and necessary administrative and
evaluation costs.
Subdivision (f) describes how the Department of Finance must report annually to the
Legislature regarding the Reserve Fund, including the Fund balance, the estimated
revenue to be generated for the Fund and proposed expenditures from the Fund. The
Department also shall verify that moneys from the Reserve Fund are not being used to
replace existing state funding. After the Director of Finance determines that all revenues
from the Act have been collected and spent, under subdivision (g) the Legislature has the
authority to abolish the Reserve Fund. Subdivision (h) provides definitions for this
section.
4
Sec. 6. Operative Tax Provisions
Part. 27. 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
Chapter 1. Imposition of Tax on Personal Wealth in Excess of $1 Billion in Net
Worth
Section 50300. Short title
Provides that Part 27 is known, and may be cited, as the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Section 50301. Imposition of tax; rate and phase-in; payment; filing; audit
Subdivision (a): One-time excise tax; determination dates; married couples.
This subdivision imposes, for tax year 2026, an excise tax on the “activity of sustaining
excessive accumulations of wealth” by California residents with worldwide net worth of
$1 billion or more. Net worth includes all assets, whether tangible or financial, except for
certain exceptions described in more detail below. Recent data suggest as much as three-
quarters of current billionaire wealth is in the form of stock of publicly-traded companies.
In order to prevent the misuse of trusts to avoid the tax, this subdivision also imposes tax
on any trust to which a living California billionaire has transferred assets; these trusts are
described in more detail in Section 50308 below.
Whether a person is a California resident is determined as of the “tax obligation date”
(January 1, 2026), while the amount of net worth subject to tax is measured as of the
“valuation date” (December 31, 2026). The timing for determining whether a trust is an
applicable trust is discussed under Section 50308 below.
Subdivision (b): 5% tax; phase-in between $1.0B and $1.1B; ODA carve-out.
• Tax rate. This subdivision sets the tax rate at 5% of net worth for individuals with
net worth in excess of $1 billion and covered trusts. For fairness, the full rate
phases in linearly for taxpayers with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion
(with respect to individuals other than trusts).
• Deferral for illiquid taxpayers. Allows an individual who lacks current liquid
assets to pay the tax to opt to initiate an Optional Deferral Account (“ODA”)
under Section 50304 to defer paying tax until the time specified by Section 50304.
ODAs are discussed in greater detail in Section 50304.
Subdivision (c): Return filing and timing; installment option and deferral charge.
This subdivision provides that additional tax payable under Section 50301 (and under
Section 50304 [the ODA provision], if applicable) is reported with, and due at the same
time as, the taxpayer’s annual personal income tax return. A taxpayer may either pay the
tax in full with the 2026 return or elect to pay in five equal annual installments beginning
5
in the year the tax is due. Each subsequent annual installment is subject to an annual
nondeductible “deferral charge” equal to 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.
Subdivision (d): Filing requirement / certification.
This subdivision requires every California resident individual who files an income tax
return for 2026 to either (i) make a simple declaration as part of the individual’s annual
tax filings (like the checkbox declarations of a taxpayer’s filing status or dependent
status) that the individual’s net assets were less than or equal to $1 billion as of the
valuation date or (ii) submit a declaration of the additional tax owed under Part 27,
together with required Board forms and supporting valuation evidence (including
certified appraisals where required).
Subdivision (e): Franchise Tax Board examination obligation and powers.
This subdivision directs the Board to examine all returns submitted under Part 27 and to
determine the correct amount of tax owed by billionaires. The Board is not required to
audit taxpayers who check the box to indicate they are not billionaires and is granted no
new authority for audits generally. There are not expected to be many such returns and
the FTB will be given more resources (see proposed Government Code Section 16355(e)
above), and time to complete audits (see Section 50309(b)(3)). Subdivision (e)(2)
specifies that the Board has discretion over the length of any such audit.
Chapter 2. Computation of Net Worth
Section 50302. Debts and liabilities
• Calculation of net worth. Prop 40 imposes a tax on a taxpayer’s net worth and
thus the Act reduces, with certain limitations, the taxable wealth by the amount of
any liability that is personally owed by the taxpayer. Legally enforceable
charitable pledges entered into before October 15, 2025 also reduce net worth.
• Genuine debts and certain other liabilities reduce net worth. Debt can be used to
artificially reduce taxpayer net worth to an extent that does not reflect economic
reality, however. Thus, the amount of any nonrecourse or limited recourse debt
that reduces net worth may not exceed the value included in the taxpayer’s net
worth for the collateral securing that debt. For the same reasons, contingent
liabilities, liabilities owed to related parties or otherwise not at arms’ length, and
debts with an interest rate below market generally do not reduce net worth. Other
liabilities entered into for the purpose of reducing tax may also be disregarded
under the general anti-avoidance rules described in Section 50312, below.
Section 50303. Valuation rules; exclusions; asset-type rules
Subdivision (a): Fair market value standard.
Adopts, with certain technical modifications, the standard tax definition of fair market
value: the price a willing and informed buyer would pay a willing and informed seller.
6
Subdivision (b): Anti-abuse rules.
Disallows certain legal structures taxpayers commonly use to reduce the taxable value of
an asset. In particular, this section is intended to disallow two common techniques used
by very wealthy taxpayers to reduce the valuation of an estate that would otherwise be
subject to estate tax. The drafters specifically intend that prior opinions of the U.S. Tax
Court upholding these techniques, which commenters generally agree were wrongly
decided, should not govern interpretation of Prop 40.
Subdivision (c): Asset-type valuation rules, exclusions, and reporting requirements.
This subdivision provides default valuation methods, exclusions, and reporting
requirements for specific asset types.
1. Publicly traded assets — “market trading value on the valuation date” (Section
50303(c)(1))
For all publicly traded assets, fair market value is presumed to be the asset’s market
trading value on December 31, 2026. The drafters expect that assets that are not publicly
traded but readily convertible to a publicly traded asset will have a value of not less than
the value of the publicly traded asset.
Prop 40 uses market pricing on the valuation date of December 31, 2026 for publicly
traded assets because those assets have readily ascertainable values through active
markets, reducing the need for appraisal-based valuation and lowering administrative and
compliance costs. Also, a taxpayer has the option of selling a portion of such assets on
the valuation date to effectively lock in the market value on the valuation date. Although
Prop 40 does not specify the precise convention for determining “market trading value”
(for example, closing price, a volume-weighted average price, the mean of high and low
prices, or a bid/ask midpoint when no trades occur), the Board may specify such
conventions by regulation or other guidance, including rules for thin trading, multiple
exchanges, and days on which there is no trading. In that respect, federal estate and gift
tax valuation precedents for publicly traded securities (particularly Treasury Regulation
§§ 20.2031-2 and 25.2512-2) provide a reasonable reference point for these valuation
issues. The Board has general authority to promulgate such guidance under Section
50309(b), but is also specifically instructed to look to federal regulations in a related
context at Section 50305(b).
2. Sole proprietorships (Section 50303(c)(2))
Treats assets held through a sole proprietorship as directly owned and held by the
taxpayer.
3. Non-public business entity interests — “Presumed Percentage Method” and rebuttable
presumptions (Section 50303(c)(3))
Governs valuation of interests in business entities (including equity, debt, and other
contractual or noncontractual interests) that are not (i) interests in publicly traded
7
companies; or (ii) sole proprietorship assets. These default rules are designed to reduce
compliance and audit costs by allowing valuation based on standardized information
from financial statements. These simplified values are presumptions for administrative
convenience. For assets or circumstances in which the simplified presumptive formulaic
valuations would be inaccurate, however, either the taxpayer or the Board may rebut
those presumptions using certified appraisals. The operation of the presumptive valuation
method is detailed in Section 50303(c)(3)(A)–(E).
• Reporting inputs (Section 50303(c)(3)(A)–(B)).
In order to assess whether the presumptive formulas have been applied accurately,
the taxpayer must report the relevant underlying financial information. Note that
this information has been chosen to be of a type that is ordinarily produced by a
business in any event. If the taxpayer lacks the information and lacks the right to
obtain it, the taxpayer must submit a certified appraisal of all of the taxpayer’s
interests in the entity.
• Presumed Percentage Method — ownership percentage presumptions and
valuation formula (Section 50303(c)(3)(C)–(E)).
Subparagraph E contains a simple formula for calculating the value of interests in
non-public entities based on standard financial information. Subparagraphs C, D,
and the end of E contain additional presumptions applicable to special cases of
non-public entities. Taxpayers who are unsatisfied with the value determined
under the formula and its presumptions may instead elect to submit an appraisal.
If there is clear and convincing evidence that the appraised value is a more
accurate measure of value, it will govern.
• Entity value formula (beginning of E): The fair market value of the taxpayer’s
interest is presumed to equal: (Entity GAAP book value at year-end + 7.5 ×
average GAAP book profits) × (taxpayer’s percentage owned). Average book
profits are computed over the current tax year and the preceding two tax years, if
available. Negative average profits are treated as zero. The Board may permit
consistent non-GAAP accounting methods where appropriate.
• Control-rights floor (C): For interests conferring voting or other direct control
rights, the taxpayer’s “percentage owned” is presumed to be at least the
taxpayer’s percentage of overall voting or other direct control rights. This
presumption addresses a tax planning technique common in the context of the
estate tax.3 It does not apply to interests in publicly traded entities.

There’s no denying the visceral satisfaction of a billionaire bloodletting. But will the measure’s wealth tax actually help the state?
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:42 p.m.
Taxation, like everything else in life, is an exercise in trade-offs.
How much public good can a tax extract before it passes the tipping point into harm?
As it relates to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php) on California’s November ballot, many believe you don’t have to look very hard to find where the cost-benefit needle falls.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on anyone whose total net worth is greater than $1 billion as of Dec. 31, 2026, and who was a California resident on Jan. 1, 2026. After administrative costs, 90% of the revenue would go to public healthcare, while the other 10% would go to food assistance and education. The total collected could range from $28 billion to $100 billion — depending on whose math you believe. (California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the state will “probably” (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) collect “tens of billions.”)

Whatever the total, there’s no denying that California billionaires — who by some counts control a combined $2 trillion (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) in wealth — can afford to shoulder it.
Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and a coauthor of Prop 40, called the measure a “rounding error” on the fortunes of California’s wealthiest.
For this mostly bloodless toll, Californians get relief from President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful” Medicaid cuts and radiate with satisfaction at sending a landmark message about wealth inequality.
Or so it would seem.

Is Prop 40 so flawlessly executed that California has nothing to lose if it passes?
Opposition from the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood, California Medical Association, the NAACP, California Professional Firefighters and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California suggests not.
Let’s start with the healthcare organizations, which would effectively receive 90% of Prop 40’s funds. Why are they opposed?
Dustin Corcoran, CEO of the California Medical Association, said in an endorsement interview that there’s no guarantee Prop 40’s payload will arrive in time to backfill Trump’s cuts. The state has no existing system for assessing billionaire wealth, he said, and it will likely take years to develop one.
Corcoran cited his experience as a backer of Prop 56, which passed in 2016 and imposed a tax on vape products.

“It probably took the Franchise Tax Board 10 years of us beating them up because they couldn’t figure out how to get the tax right,” he said. “And that was a fairly straightforward thing to try and figure out.”
Even if the money does land, and that’s a big if, Corcoran argued that weak “anti-supplantation” protections in the measure will allow lawmakers to spend its revenue however they see fit — undermining one of Prop 40’s most powerful arguments, the urgency of the moment for healthcare.
University of Missouri School of Law Professor David Gamage, one of Prop 40’s coauthors, disputed these notions. He estimated that “75% of billionaire wealth is in publicly traded assets,” making much of it easy to track. And even if the measure does have supplantation holes, political pressure will prevent California politicians from treating Prop 40 revenue like a slush fund.
These vague assurances don’t persuade Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Healthcare organizations like hers, she said, use forward-looking budgets. They can’t commit to providing services if they can’t definitively rely on money coming in to pay for them.
Meanwhile, Prop 40 puts the money Hicks can count on in jeopardy.

That’s because California’s budget is overly dependent on income taxes — roughly half of which (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/7)historically come from the ultra-wealthy top 1% of taxpayers.
Studying the impacts of Prop 40 “was an eye-opening experience for what California’s tax structure is and how the wealthy are a part of it,” Hicks said.
This gets at the real questions surrounding Prop 40 and why so many otherwise progressive organizations oppose the tax: Will billionaires leave the state if the measure passes, and will they take their companies with them?
“Good riddance” is the popular retort among online commentators.
But that attitude is childish and self-defeating. A recent case study explained why.

The world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, left California in 2020, citing high taxes as one of his reasons. He took Tesla’s corporate headquarters with him to Texas the following year.
By some estimates, California lost an estimated $2.5 billion (https://www.businessinsider.com/why-did-elon-musk-move-texas-wealth-tax-capital-gains-2021-11) in capital gains revenue from one stock transaction in the first year of Musk’s move. In a state where 40% of state dollars are required by law to go to public education, that’s a $1 billion hole in California’s school budget from one man alone.
This answers why the formidable California Teachers Association — never one to shy away from a back-alley tax brawl — doesn’t support Prop 40.
Then there are the jobs.
Many Tesla workers stayed behind in California. But new Tesla jobs are now sprouting up across Texas, including nearly 10,000 for a proposed $10 billion solar cell factory (https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/09/18/teslas-10-1-billion-texas-solar-gigafactory-clears-key-tax-hurdle/).
You’ve heard the aphorism, “Keep your friends close and your enemies closer.” Here’s a real-world example of why.
Sending billionaires and the jobs and economic might that come with them to Texas or Florida does not help California. Nor does it help the prospects for building a more just society. It simply makes those red states more powerful.
So, will Prop 40 send billionaires fleeing?
A working paper from Stanford says yes, (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) and argues that exodus will result in a net tax revenue loss of nearly $39 billion for California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Indeed, some billionaires — most famously Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has dumped hundreds of millions into opposing Prop 40 — have already announced their departures.
Some economists dispute the Stanford study (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988796082176375), arguing it ignores basic human motivation. Prop 40 will hit any billionaire who lived in California as of Jan. 1. Why would they uproot their lives now over a one-time tax they have to pay regardless — especially one they can easily afford?
We’d counter that California’s nation-leading 13.3% marginal income tax rate — necessary as it may be (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php), given our state’s finances — already poses a flight risk. Even Gamage said he was “uncomfortable” (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) with the top rate. A wealth tax merely compounds a danger that already exists.
It’s true that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has committed to ponying up (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/billionaires-fight-tax-hike-jensen-160907521.html) his estimated $8 billion in dues. And Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has apparently agreed to stay in California for eight years after strong-arming the company (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php#:~:text=Meta%20revealed%20in%20a%20Securities%20and%20Exchange%20Commission%20filing%20that%20Mark%20Zuckerberg%20was%20considering%20leaving%20California%2C%20but%20agreed%20to%20stay%20after%20the%20company%20gave%20him%20a%20new%20stock%20deal) into eating his wealth tax burden.
Yet the debate around flight risk has largely focused on the wealthiest of the wealthy. Less discussed are the paper billionaires — those with unrealized stakes in valuable startups and other private companies.
Prop 40’s method for assessing this wealth (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan) is dubious. Some believe the measure allows voting shares or control percentage to be used in calculating wealth, rather than ownership stake, which could be wildly off. The measure does offer a mechanism for the wealthy to contest their asset valuations, but at what point are companies going to decide enough is enough and seek their fortunes elsewhere?
“Only idiot startup founders stay in Cali” if Prop 40 passes, billionaire investor Mark Cuban has said on social media. (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan?utm_source=chatgpt.com) “You can bet if I’m investing in a multi-billion-dollar startup, I’m asking them to move from California first.”
“Boo hoo,” you say?
California’s startup culture is a crucial engine of its economy. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, companies in the state receive nearly half of all American venture capital (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2024/4942/CalFacts-2024-120224.pdf). Another study found these investments help employ 1.2 million people (https://www.nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/California-VC-State-Data.pdf). As companies grow their roots, California’s budget sees the benefit.
Many argue that the talent ecosystem in California makes an exodus impossible.
But people said the same thing about Hollywood for decades. Now the entertainment industry is shedding thousands of jobs to states like Georgia and North Carolina that offer more favorable economic incentives.
If movie titans are willing to abandon a company town practically built to indulge their excess, it’s not a stretch to imagine a significant portion of the tech universe fleeing to Miami or Austin, where workforce housing is cheaper, they would pay no state income tax, and the sword of future wealth taxes would no longer hang over their endeavors.
All this speaks to why tackling extreme wealth is better approached at the federal level. There’s evidence from Spain and elsewhere that the wealthy will shop around regionally (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to) for lower taxes. There’s much less evidence that they’ll flee the country.
We are already seeing momentum for a federal inequality crackdown. Democrats are poised to retake Congress, and Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Burbank, recently announced legislation that would impose an excise tax of 23.8% (https://news.bgov.com/bloomberg-government-news/house-democrat-pitches-new-wealth-tax-as-midterms-draw-near) on most line-of-credit loans — which are leveraged against assets like stocks — above $1 million.
Ever wonder how the Zuckerbergs of the world get by on a salary of $1? Borrowing against stock gives them access to cash without having to pay capital gains. In fact, in some cases, interest payments on these loans are tax deductible under federal policy.
Fixing these loopholes would force the ultra-wealthy to either take salaries or liquidate assets when they need cash, which would mean income tax boons for states like California.
Obviously, with Trump still in charge, it could take a few years for these and other changes to manifest.
Instead of being patient, however, Prop 40 throws the full weight of risk on California’s shoulders now.
“Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?”
We wholeheartedly agree with these sentiments, espoused by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders at a recent rally in support of Prop 40.
But living up to them demands strategic thinking, not primal screaming.
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be.
Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tLQFHYqkVtY)
It just happens to be one dropped into the maw of the world’s fourth-largest economy — a wealthy state in aggregate, but one with a volatile, incoherent system of taxation (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php) and the highest poverty rate in the nation.
If Prop 40 backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. Our sales and income taxes are already the highest in the nation; there’s no more room for hikes. Meanwhile, Prop 13 stunts our ability to raise new revenue from property taxes.
No one is coming to save us. And it won’t be the wealthy who suffer.
Maybe, just maybe, the stakes are too high in California to be playing a game of chicken. Maybe the brightest and boldest minds in the field of economic justice should help stabilize California’s tax base before turning our state into a laboratory?

Billionaire Tax Explained: What Proposition 40 Would Mean for California
Implications of the One-Time Billionaire Wealth Tax for Californians
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires to raise tens of billions in temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding and other threats to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of H.R. 1 — the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services, but may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax.
table of contents
Background
Who Would Be Subject to the Tax Under Prop. 40 and How Would It Be Calculated?
What Is the Difference Between Income and Wealth?
How Is Wealth Distributed Across California?
How Much Revenue Will Prop. 40 Raise?
What Would Prop. 40 Funds Pay For?
How Would Prop. 40 Revenues Impact Californians?
What Are the Concerns About Prop. 40?
How Do Props. 41 and 42 Conflict With Prop. 40 on the November Ballot?
The Bottom Line on Prop. 40
Prop. 40 Supporters and Opponents
Background
California, like many other states, is facing a number of challenges to its ability to meet the needs of its residents, including the impending impacts of the deep federal cuts to public health care and nutrition assistance (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/) and the rising costs of providing services due to inflation, an aging population with more complex needs, and the state’s ongoing housing crisis. The federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are expected to cost the state tens of billions of dollars in lost funding and could lead to around 1.3 million Californians losing health care access by 2029-30. Meaningfully addressing these challenges will require California to raise a substantial amount of revenue (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
what is h.r. 1?
H.R. 1, the 2025 budget reconciliation law known (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” signed by President Trump on July 4, 2025, will deeply harm Californians by cutting funding for essential health care and food assistance programs — while providing massive tax breaks to the wealthy and corporations. The spending cuts will disproportionately impact families with low incomes, immigrants, and communities of color, pushing more people into poverty and widening racial and economic inequities across the state.
Even prior to these more recent challenges, California was not generating enough revenue to meet the critical needs of all Californians through the state’s communities, evidenced by the state’s poverty rate remaining the highest in the nation (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-persistent-poverty-crisis-2024-rates-remain-alarmingly-high/). In addition to the human suffering caused by failing to ensure Californians can regularly access health care, put enough food on the table, and meet their other basic needs, such a failure dampens the state economy by preventing some individuals from fully participating in it and puts fiscal pressures on state and local governments as more households are forced to turn to costly emergency services and systems of last resort.
In the near term, Prop. 40 would likely generate tens of billions in revenue to prevent health coverage losses for Californians and stabilize the state’s health care system, and could provide additional support for nutrition assistance — which is also impacted by federal cuts — and for public education. Because the revenues would be one-time, the state would not be able to maintain these services in the future unless federal funding were fully restored or the state adopted alternative sources to raise this magnitude of revenue.
There is a strong rationale for taxing accumulated wealth — or taxing increases in wealth that currently go untaxed — given the profound wealth inequality and the vast unmet needs that exist in the state and across the country, as well as the ability of some ultrawealthy households to pay very little in income taxes as a share of their wealth.
At the same time, taxing wealth at the state level comes with some risks, particularly the potential for wealthy people to leave the state to avoid the tax, which would result in future state income tax losses if they did not return — putting at risk future funding for critical state services — and potential unknown impacts on the state economy. Prop. 40 attempts to counter that risk by applying the tax to billionaires who were California residents at the beginning of 2026, however it is likely this will be challenged in courts and the outcome is not certain.
In November, California voters will need to weigh the potential benefits of Prop. 40 against its potential tradeoffs.
Who Would Be Subject to the Tax Under Prop. 40 and How Would It Be Calculated?
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time tax on the worldwide wealth of billionaires. For the purposes of the measure, a billionaire subject to the tax could be an individual, a married couple, or a trust with net worth — as defined by the measure — above $1 billion. There are around250 billionaires in California, with over $2 trillion in total wealth (https://cabillionairetracker.org/). 1 (javascript:void(0)) Forbes tracks the daily wealth of billionaires with its “Real-Time Billionaires” list, and the California-specific data was compiled in connection with Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman, California Billionaires: Wealth, Taxes, and Wealth Tax Revenue Estimates (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/BSZ26CAbillionaires.pdf) (NBER Working Paper 35218, May 2026). Note: Saez is an author of Prop. 40.
The tax rate would be 5% for most billionaires, but the rate would be phased in for those with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. 2 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, the 5% rate would be reduced by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million that the household’s net worth falls below $1.1 billion. Taxpayers would have the option of paying the full amount of the tax with their 2026 tax returns or in installments across five years, with an annual deferral charge.
Net worth is typically calculated as the total value of assets held by an individual, couple, or family minus their total debts. However, Prop. 40 allows some exclusions from the net worth calculation, including:
Real property holdings, which are subject to constitutional tax limitations due to Proposition 13, approved by California voters in 1978;
Tangible personal property — such as vehicles, jewelry, appliances, or business equipment — held outside of California; 3 (javascript:void(0)) Tangible personal property is excluded from the net worth calculation if it is held outside of California for at least 270 days during 2026 unless it was temporarily relocated for the purpose of tax avoidance. and
Certain pensions, retirement accounts, and deferred compensation arrangements.
The measure would apply the tax to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, and the amounts subject to the tax would be determined based on their net worth on December 31, 2026. There will likely be legal challenges to the application of the tax based on residency prior to the enactment of the tax. Federal and state tax measures often have retroactivity provisions to minimize tax avoidance and courts have upheld many of these laws, although it is unknown how courts would ultimately rule on this measure. The measure specifies that in the case the residency and valuation dates are invalidated by courts, these dates shall be construed to be the earliest dates consistent with law.
Prop. 40 establishes procedures for estimating the value of various types of assets that would be included in net worth for the purpose of the tax. Valuation is simple for some assets, such as holdings of publicly traded stock, which have a known market value at any given time. Other assets, such as shares of private businesses, intellectual property such as copyrights or trademarks, and artwork, are more difficult to value without a sale taking place. The measure has detailed valuation rules and formulas for different types of assets, and both the taxpayer and the state’s Franchise Tax Board — which would be responsible for administering the tax — could obtain certified appraisals in the case of valuation disputes. Additionally, the measure contains provisions intended to minimize the ability of taxpayers to avoid or evade their tax responsibility. 4 (javascript:void(0)) Tax avoidance reflects legal avenues to reducing tax liability, such as redirecting wealth holdings to exempted assets or relocating, whereas tax evasion encompasses illegal tactics to avoid taxes, such as hiding assets in tax havens, underreporting of asset values, or falsely claiming residency outside of the tax jurisdiction.
Example: Potential Impact of Prop. 40 on Mark Zuckerberg
Mark Zuckerberg, cofounder of Facebook, has a net worth of around $200 billion (https://www.forbes.com/profile/mark-zuckerberg/?ctpv=rtb&list=rtb). Assuming he has approximately $200 billion in wealth subject to Prop. 40 on December 31, 2026, when net worth is to be determined for the purpose of the measure, he would owe around $10 billion in tax, which he could pay in five annual installments of $2 billion. His remaining wealth of around $190 billion would still be more than the entire economies of dozens of countries, roughly on par with (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?most_recent_value_desc=true) the Gross Domestic Product of Morocco.
For comparison, Zuckerberg’s net worth increased 175% from 2023 to 2024 (https://www.forbes.com/profile/mark-zuckerberg/?ctpv=rtb&list=rtb) according to Forbes data, from $64.4 billion to $177 billion.
What Is the Difference Between Income and Wealth?
Capital Gains: Increases in Wealth
Households holding assets that have increased in value pay federal and state tax on those gains only when they sell those assets. This is known as a realized capital gain.
However, the value of an asset can grow exponentially and go untaxed as long as it is held onto — an unrealized capital gain. While the household doesn’t directly receive the proceeds from the gain until selling the asset, unrealized capital gains represent an increase in the household’s wealth and financial well-being (https://www.cbpp.org/research/federal-tax/arguments-against-taxing-unrealized-capital-gains-of-very-wealthy-fall-flat).
For ultra-wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. 5 (javascript:void(0)) For example, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy estimated (https://itep.org/the-geographic-distribution-of-extreme-wealth-in-the-u-s/#:~:text=This%20ratio%20increases%20at%20higher%20levels%20of%20wealth%2C%20with%20unrealized%20gains%20making%20up%20almost%2070%20percent%20of%20billionaire%20wealth.) that unrealized capital gains represent nearly 70% of total wealth for billionaires. In some cases, ultra-wealthy households — such as corporate founders — can avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills. There is evidence of some of the wealthiest Americans engaging in this behavior, detailed in analyses of leaked tax returns by investigative journalists (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax), although recent research suggests (https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/richs-real-tax-trick-isnt-buy-borrow-die) that this is not a widespread phenomenon and that overall, wealthy households do have significant taxable income and their incomes allow them to cover their expenses while continuing to invest and grow their wealth.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis (https://www.pgpf.org/article/what-is-the-stepped-up-basis-and-how-does-it-affect-the-federal-budget/),” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year. 6 (javascript:void(0)) Department of Finance, Tax Expenditure Report: 2025-26 (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/forecasting/revenue-and-taxation/tax-expenditure-reports/2025-26-Tax-Expenditure-Report.pdf), p. 24. Note that the estimated annual cost of the provision is not equivalent to the revenue that could be generated from repealing it, and for this provision the revenue gains from repeal would start in the low hundreds of millions (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/797#:~:text=Eliminate%20Capital%20Gains%20Step%2DUp%20Basis%20on%20Inherited%20Assets.) and increase with time, potentially reaching $5 billion annually in the future. Essentially, the combination of unrealized capital gains not being taxed and stepped-up basis results in some large wealth increases never being taxed.
How Is Wealth Distributed Across California?
Across the country, the gaps in income (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#range:1989,2022;series:Before_Tax_Income;demographic:inccat;population:all;units:median) and wealth (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#range:1989,2022;series:Net_Worth;demographic:nwcat;population:all;units:median) have steadily grown with the top 10% of households seeing substantial growth in both income and wealth accumulation. Similarly, in California, only a tiny fraction of the population benefits from extreme income and wealth.
While both wealth and income inequality are prevalent in the state, wealth is even more unequally distributed (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=%C2%A0This%20difference%20is%20higher%20than%20in%20the%20rest%20of%20the%20country%2C%20where%20the%2080th%20percentile%20is%2099%20times%20the%2020th%2C%20and%20higher%20than%20income%20inequality%20in%20California.) than income in California. While the state has more wealth than the rest of the country (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/), the disparities in wealth are also starkest in California.
When focusing on the wealth distribution in the state, the data show an alarming gap between households with high and low wealth. Specifically, the wealthiest 20% of households have a net worth of over $1.5 million (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=High%20net%20worth%20households%20have%20substantially%20more%20wealth%20than%20low%20net%20worth%20households.), while the bottom 20% of households have a net worth of $13,000 or less. Those who would be subject to the Prop. 40 tax — those with a net worth above $1 billion — have a net worth of over 3,000 times the median household.
Wealth is also unequally distributed across racial and ethnic groups. For example, the median net worth of white households in 2023 was almost ten times (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=Net%20worth%20is%20highest%20among%20older%2C%20college%2Deducated%2C%20and%20white%20and%20Asian%20households.) the median net worth of Latinx households, reflecting the historical barriers to wealth accumulation (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) these communities have faced. Black, Latinx, and other households of color often have less wealth due to many factors including a lower likelihood of owning stocks (https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/03/06/a-booming-us-stock-market-doesnt-benefit-all-racial-and-ethnic-groups-equally/), occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) pushing them into lower-payer jobs, and a lack of inherited generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/). These factors likely contribute to the large wealth disparities that have persisted throughout history.
How Much Revenue Will Prop. 40 Raise?
There is a high degree of uncertainty in estimating the potential revenue from this measure since it is impossible to accurately predict how billionaires and the courts will respond to the tax. It is likely there will be some avoidance and evasion of the tax, as billionaires may hide or underreport their assets, shift their asset holdings toward those that are exempt from the tax, attempt to sever their ties with California, or engage in other tactics to minimize or eliminate their tax liability.
After attempting to account for these factors, the Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the billionaire tax would likely raise “tens of billions” of dollars in the near term. I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me consider a few more angles before deciding:

1. The strongest YES case:
- Genuine fiscal emergency: ~$100B in federal cuts to Medi-Cal, CalFresh, education from H.R.1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act). 1.3-3.4 million Californians could lose coverage. 145,000 healthcare jobs at risk.
- Billionaires pay a lower effective tax rate than average taxpayers relative to economic income.
- The tax is one-time, 5% — small relative to billionaire wealth growth (7%/year).
- LAO (nonpartisan) says "tens of billions" in temporary revenue, and only "less than $1 billion per year" ongoing income tax decrease — i.e., the nonpartisan estimate is net positive, contrary to the Hoover estimate.
- Bernie Sanders, CA Democratic Party, CA Labor Federation, AFSCME, Teamsters, United Teachers LA support.
- Wealth tax at federal level is stalled; states are laboratories.
- Jensen Huang said he'll pay; Zuckerberg agreed to stay.

2. The strongest NO case:
- Severe legal vulnerabilities: retroactivity/due process, Commerce Clause nexus & fair apportionment (100% of worldwide net worth with no apportionment), taxation of federal obligations (US Treasuries), Excessive Fines for appraiser penalties, intangible property tax limits (Prop 13/Art XIII A) requiring the constitutional amendment to succeed. Tax Foundation lists 8+ vulnerabilities and says reformation can't cure them.
- Even the neutral LAO says the amount and timing are "very hard to predict."
- Base erosion already occurred: ~30% of the billionaire wealth base ($540B) left before the Jan 1, 2026 residency cutoff. Tax attorneys report "a third to half" of their clients left.
- Hoover/NBER (Rauh & Jaros) estimate ~$30B gross, and a net present-value LOSS of $38.9B once lost income tax revenue from departures is counted; in 100,000 simulations, 85% of scenarios were net losses.
- Structural budget risk: California derives ~half of personal income tax revenue from the top 1%. Driving out the wealthiest taxpayers is a permanent, compounding loss against a one-time gain.
- One-time revenue for ongoing obligations = fiscal cliff. Once health providers build budgets on it, the money disappears after 5 years.
- It exempts itself from Prop 98 (school funding guarantee), the Gann appropriations limit (Art. XIII B), the rainy-day reserves (Art. XVI §8/8.5), and Prop 63 mental health tax. Those were voter-approved accountability structures.
- Weak anti-supplanting guardrails; 90% to "health care" broadly defined could go to insurers, pharma, for-profit hospitals. LA Times: "insufficient guardrails."
- The healthcare providers who'd receive the money (CMA, Children's Hospital Association, Primary Care Association, Planned Parenthood) oppose it — because timing/certainty is unreliable and forward-looking budgets can't be built on it.
- Progressive/civil rights opposition: NAACP California/Hawaii, Equality California, SF Democratic Party, CTA, Professional Firefighters, Building Trades.
- Valuation of private companies (VC-backed) is dubious and would create huge compliance disputes and possibly misvalue assets; penalties on appraisers are uncapped.
- Precedent: ballot-box budgeting by a single interest group (SEIU-UHW) targeting a politically unpopular class and dedicating proceeds to its own preferred programs.
- Every major newspaper editorial board in CA (LA Times, SF Chronicle, Bay Area News Group/Mercury News, Sac Bee) says NO.
- Even the drafters admit it's an "experiment" on the world's 4th largest economy.
- Better alternative: pursue wealth-tax/borrow-against-stock loophole fixes at federal level, where capital cannot flee across state lines. Also Prop 3 on the same ballot (high-income tax) exists.

3. The "loophole" claim (Legislature could extend to everyone): partially true but overstated; the tax is in the constitution, and amendments must "further the purposes," so extending to non-billionaires would likely need another ballot measure. I should not rely on that claim.

Weighing: The core question is whether a one-time, retroactive, unapportioned, first-in-the-nation state wealth tax with severe constitutional vulnerabilities, applied after ~30% of the base has already fled, and which creates a fiscal cliff while exempting itself from Prop 98/Gann/reserve protections, is a net positive for California.

The nonpartisan LAO gives a net-positive but highly uncertain estimate. The independent Hoover/NBER analysis gives a net-negative. But note: the LAO is the official referee, and it doesn't do the net-loss calculation. However, the LAO's "possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year" is itself a meaningful permanent hit — and it's about ongoing, recurring revenue being traded for one-time revenue.

Important asymmetry: Even if the tax raises $30B over 5 years, that's one-time. If it costs $1-3.5B/year in income tax permanently, within ~10-30 years the loss exceeds the gain. And critically, ~30% of the base already fled — that damage is largely done whether or not Prop 40 passes (it happened in response to the initiative's filing). But passing it locks in the flight incentive going forward and signals future wealth taxes, whereas rejecting it removes that signal.

Hmm, but a counter: since the flight already happened, passing Prop 40 now collects from those who stayed (Huang, Zuckerberg who agreed to stay, etc.) without much additional marginal flight. That's the Zucman/Saez argument: it's retroactive to Jan 1, 2026, so those covered must pay regardless of whether they now leave. So the marginal cost of a yes vote is lower than it appears, and the marginal benefit is tens of billions for healthcare.

That's a genuinely strong argument. But: (a) it assumes the tax survives court review — a big assumption given the constitutional problems; (b) even if the covered billionaires can't escape the one-time tax by leaving now, their departure still costs California their future income taxes, jobs, companies, VC ecosystem — which is precisely what the retroactivity cannot recapture; (c) the retroactive reach to former residents is itself one of the most legally vulnerable features (due process/nexus), so the people most likely to be captured by it are also the most likely to successfully sue; and (d) it creates the fiscal cliff and exempts itself from budget guardrails.

Also worth noting: the "money for healthcare" framing. The measure dedicates revenue but with weak guardrails and it's one-time while Medi-Cal's need is ongoing ($8.6B/year structural shortfall from 2028-29 onward). So it doesn't solve the problem it's marketed as solving; it delays it by five years and then makes it worse.

Additionally, there's a real risk that a "yes" vote here doesn't even achieve the goal because of Props 41/42 — but that's not a reason to vote no on 40 per se.

Let me also weigh: is there any evidence that the tax will be struck down, or has a court ruled? Let me check quickly whether there's been a pre-election court decision. Also, let me verify the Tax Foundation's specific claims about federal obligations (US Treasuries being included), since that's a serious drafting defect.

Let me do a couple more targeted checks, then decide.

Actually, one more important consideration: the measure taxes "worldwide net worth" with no apportionment. Under the Commerce Clause's Complete Auto test, a state tax must be fairly apportioned. Prop 40 taxes 100% of worldwide wealth including assets with no California connection. That's a serious problem — and the drafters' response is that it's an "excise tax on the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth," which courts may or may not accept. Also, states are constitutionally barred from taxing federal obligations (intergovernmental tax immunity) — if US Treasuries are included, that's a defect.

Let me verify these two points and check for any court rulings.
